title: Episode 16: Issue Templates
description: Creating YAML-based issue templates for bug reports, features, and custom forms.
concepts: What issue templates are and why projects use them
YAML front matter: name, description, title, labels, assignees
Markdown body templates with placeholder sections
Creating a bug report template with steps to reproduce
Creating custom templates for any purpose
The template chooser page: what users see when filing an issue
config.yml: adding external links and configuring the chooser
Form-based templates: input types (textarea, input, dropdown, checkboxes)
Validation and required fields in form templates
How templates improve issue quality and reduce back-and-forth
Testing your templates by filing an issue
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're talking about issue templates, and this is one of those topics that sounds administrative until you realize it can completely change how accessible and useful contribution workflows feel.

[JAMIE]
Yes. A blank issue box can feel like someone saying, "Tell me everything," with no structure, no prompts, and no clue what matters.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Templates turn that blank box into guidance. They help contributors include the right details, help maintainers spend less time asking follow-up questions, and help projects get to action faster. And for accessibility work, structure matters even more, because missing environment details, assistive technology details, or reproduction steps can make a report much harder to use.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A quick orientation before we go deeper. This lesson connects to a few other parts of your learning path. You should already know how to work with GitHub issues, and it helps if you have a repository where you have write access, like a fork or personal repo. You'll also want an editor that highlights YAML syntax, such as VS Code. Optional but helpful background includes GitHub Copilot, notifications, and basic terminal comfort, though you can do a lot in the browser if needed.

[JAMIE]
And there's a really practical hook here. Learners in this workshop already filled out a workshop registration template, right?

[ALEX]
Right. That registration form is not just paperwork. It is the teaching example for this lesson. You've already experienced what a polished GitHub form template feels like from the user side. Now you're going to analyze it, remix it, and potentially create your own.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a forward-looking note here. Later, in the Accessibility Agents material, there's a template builder agent that can help automate some of this. But the idea is: learn the manual structure first, then use the automation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Learn the craft before you delegate it.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Here's the overall learning path for this chapter. First, understand what templates are and why they matter. Second, learn how GitHub handles them. Third, navigate the template picker accessibly. Fourth, read a real template file. Fifth, create your own template step by step. Sixth, compare Markdown templates with YAML form templates. Seventh, build an accessibility bug report template. Eighth, look at pull request templates. Ninth, do hands-on exercises. And finally, see how the template builder agent fits in.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a challenge structure wrapped around all of that.

[ALEX]
Yes. The recommended workshop challenge for this chapter is a design-and-implementation challenge focused on template remixing. The pattern is analyze, remix, create, and test. Evidence can be an issue comment or a pull request showing what you remixed or created. There isn't an automation check here; quality is judged more by structure and thoughtfulness.

[JAMIE]
So what are the challenge pieces?

[ALEX]
There are four. Analyze the registration template. Remix it for a different use case. Optionally create a Markdown template from scratch. And optionally test your template in the GitHub chooser.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's start at the beginning. What is an issue template?

[ALEX]
An issue template is a reusable structure that appears when someone creates a new issue in a repository. Instead of giving people only an empty text area, GitHub can offer prepared templates that guide them through what information to provide.

[JAMIE]
So, in practice, that might mean prompts like describe the bug, list steps to reproduce, explain expected behavior, and so on.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Or for a feature request, it might ask what problem you're trying to solve, who benefits, and what alternatives you considered. The big idea is that templates create consistent, higher-quality reports.

[JAMIE]
Why does that especially matter for accessibility projects?

[ALEX]
Because accessibility issues often depend on context. A report may need the component affected, the screen reader or magnifier involved, the browser, the operating system, the keyboard steps used, what was expected, what actually happened, and maybe even a relevant WCAG success criterion if known. Without prompts, contributors may leave out critical information, not because they're careless, but because they don't know what maintainers need.

[JAMIE]
So the template is doing both instructional and organizational work.

[ALEX]
Yes. It teaches contributors what counts as a useful report while also collecting that information in a predictable format.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How do templates work on GitHub at a practical level?

[ALEX]
GitHub supports issue templates and pull request templates. For issues, repositories typically store them inside a special folder, usually .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Templates can be either Markdown files or YAML form files. GitHub reads those files and uses them to populate the issue creation experience.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a configuration file sometimes, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. A config file, commonly called config.yml in that templates area, can control behavior like whether blank issues are allowed and whether contact links appear. That means maintainers can shape the overall issue intake process, not just individual templates.

[JAMIE]
So one repo might offer several choices like bug report, feature request, accessibility issue, workshop registration, and maybe a support link.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The chooser becomes a little intake desk.

[JAMIE]
Can you give the high-level difference between Markdown templates and YAML forms right now, before we get deeper?

[ALEX]
Sure. Markdown templates are simpler text-based issue starters. They include frontmatter and then a Markdown body, often with headings and HTML comments. YAML form templates are more structured. They render actual form fields like text inputs, dropdowns, textareas, and checkboxes. YAML forms generally provide a more guided and accessible experience because each field has a clear label, description, and validation rules.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about the template picker itself, because learners will encounter that first on GitHub.com.

[ALEX]
When a repository has templates configured, selecting New Issue typically opens a chooser. You'll hear or encounter template names, short descriptions, and usually a button like Get started for each template. For screen reader users, the important strategy is to move methodically: identify the template name, listen for its description, then activate the control to start with that template.

[JAMIE]
And if there are multiple templates, those descriptions matter a lot.

[ALEX]
They do. A good description helps someone decide, "Is this for a bug, a feature idea, an accessibility problem, or something else?" Clear naming and description are accessibility features in their own right.

[JAMIE]
What about bypassing the chooser?

[ALEX]
Sometimes GitHub allows direct links that preselect templates or a blank issue option if maintainers have enabled that. But as a learner, the important thing is to understand both experiences: the chooser helps route people properly, and bypassing it may exist for advanced or direct workflows. Still, maintainers often want the chooser used because it improves consistency.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's ground this in the real example: the Accessibility Agents issue templates and especially the workshop registration template.

[ALEX]
Yes. This is a great exercise because it's a real production file, not a toy example. The first challenge is to open that template file on GitHub.com and analyze it.

[JAMIE]
What exactly should learners look for first?

[ALEX]
Start with the frontmatter at the top. In a YAML issue form, key items include name, description, title, and labels. Name is what appears in the template chooser. Description is the helper text shown there. Title can prefill the issue title or at least provide a prefix. Labels let GitHub automatically tag issues created from that template.

[JAMIE]
So right away, the template is doing organizational work before the user even fills anything out.

[ALEX]
That's right. Then look at the body section. That's where the form fields live. In the workshop registration template, you'll find field types like markdown for instructions, input for single-line entries, dropdown for fixed options, and textarea for longer responses.

[JAMIE]
And each field has metadata.

[ALEX]
Yes. This is crucial. Each field can include an id, which is the internal identifier and not typically what the user sees; a label, which is the visible field name; a description, which gives helpful guidance; a placeholder, which offers example text inside the field; and validations such as required true, which tells GitHub that the field must be completed.

[JAMIE]
That pairing of visible guidance plus required-optional clarity is really powerful.

[ALEX]
It is. And the challenge specifically asks learners to search the file for the word accessible, noticing that the template description explicitly considers screen reader usability. That models professional thinking: not just collecting data, but collecting it in a way people can successfully provide.

[JAMIE]
And then there's the comparison with a blank issue.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A blank issue is one giant invitation to guess. A template replaces guessing with structure.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's turn that into the remix challenge. Suppose a learner understands the registration template. What do they do next?

[ALEX]
They adapt it for a new context while preserving the underlying structure. This is a fantastic exercise because it teaches that good template design is partly architecture and partly content design.

[JAMIE]
What stays the same?

[ALEX]
The YAML skeleton stays the same: name, description, title, labels, body. The field structure also stays recognizable: type, id, attributes, validations.

[JAMIE]
And what changes?

[ALEX]
The context-specific parts. Change the template name and description to match the new purpose. Change the title prefix. Change labels. Rewrite each field's label, description, placeholder, and dropdown options so they fit the new workflow. And reconsider which fields should be required.

[JAMIE]
So if I remix a registration template into a bug report template, I might replace attendee details with component name, browser, screen reader, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, and actual behavior.

[ALEX]
Perfect example. And after editing, validate the YAML syntax. The lesson recommends pasting the contents into a YAML linter like yamllint.com. That catches indentation mistakes and formatting errors, which are common in YAML.

[JAMIE]
YAML is very unforgiving about spacing.

[ALEX]
It is. Small indentation errors can break a whole template.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also an optional challenge to create a Markdown template. Why include that if YAML forms are more structured?

[ALEX]
Because understanding both formats gives you flexibility. A Markdown template is simpler to create and easier to support in repositories where you want a lightweight starter rather than a full form. It also helps learners understand the evolution from freeform guidance to structured input.

[JAMIE]
What does a Markdown template look like?

[ALEX]
At the top, it has frontmatter between triple-dashed lines. Typical keys are name, about, title, and labels. One detail matters a lot here: Markdown templates use about, while YAML forms use description. That difference is easy to forget.

[JAMIE]
Good catch.

[ALEX]
Below the frontmatter comes the Markdown body. Usually that means headings like Problem, Context, and Solution Ideas, with HTML comments underneath to guide the writer without leaving visible instructional clutter in the rendered issue.

[JAMIE]
So something like a heading for Problem and then an HTML comment saying, describe the problem you encountered.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's guidance embedded in plain text structure.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we spend a moment on those example Markdown sections, because the source calls them out very specifically?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. A classic bug-style Markdown template might include sections for Describe the Bug, Steps to Reproduce, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Environment, and Additional Context.

[JAMIE]
That sequence matters, doesn't it?

[ALEX]
It does. Describe the Bug gives the summary. Steps to Reproduce makes the issue testable. Expected Behavior clarifies what should have happened. Actual Behavior records what did happen. Environment provides context like browser, operating system, app version, or assistive technology. Additional Context gives space for screenshots, logs, workarounds, or anything else.

[JAMIE]
And for accessibility-specific reporting, the source adds more focused sections.

[ALEX]
Right. You might include Component Affected, Your Assistive Technology Setup, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Steps to Reproduce, WCAG Success Criterion if known, Additional Context, and Before Submitting.

[JAMIE]
That "Before Submitting" part is interesting.

[ALEX]
It reminds contributors to do a final quality check. For example: have you reproduced the issue, provided enough detail, checked for duplicates, and included your environment? It reduces incomplete submissions.

[JAMIE]
When would you use this Markdown version instead of YAML?

[ALEX]
Use Markdown when you need a quick, portable template, when a project prefers simple text, or when the issue type benefits from freer narrative. Use YAML when you want stronger structure, clearer labels, required fields, and a more guided experience.

[JAMIE]
And there are accessibility considerations for Markdown templates too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Keep headings clear and logical. Use plain language. Don't overload the page with dense instructions. Make placeholders and comments specific but brief. And remember that Markdown templates still rely more on the contributor to interpret and follow the structure, so they are usually less constrained than YAML forms.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What are the practical workflows for creating Markdown templates?

[ALEX]
There are two main ones described. The manual browser workflow and the VS Code workflow. In the browser, you can create the file directly in GitHub's web editor inside .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. In VS Code, you create the same file locally, edit it with syntax support, then commit and push.

[JAMIE]
And file naming conventions matter.

[ALEX]
They do. Give the template a clear descriptive filename, like bug-report.md or accessibility-bug-report.yml. Good names help maintainers and collaborators understand what each file is for.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's go deeper into YAML form templates, because that seems to be the star of this chapter.

[ALEX]
I agree. YAML forms are often better for accessibility because they create explicit form controls. Users encounter labeled fields rather than a giant blank editing area. The template author can provide descriptions, placeholders, dropdown choices, and required-field validation. That reduces ambiguity and makes the reporting process more predictable.

[JAMIE]
So the accessibility benefit is not just that the content is better, but that the interaction model is clearer.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A clear form with good labels is often easier to navigate and understand than a freeform page of instructions.

[JAMIE]
What is the structure of a YAML form template?

[ALEX]
At the top level, you usually see keys like name, description, title, labels, and body. The body is a list of items, and each item has a type. Depending on the type, it may also have an id, attributes, and validations.

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through the field types one by one?

[ALEX]
Yes. First, markdown. This is instructional text only. It's used for context, reminders, or directions. It does not collect user input.

[JAMIE]
So that's good for a short introduction or a note about checking for duplicate issues first.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Second, input. That's a single-line text field. Use it for concise information like component names, email addresses, version numbers, or short summaries.

[JAMIE]
Third is textarea.

[ALEX]
Right. Textarea is for multi-line responses. Use it when contributors need room to explain steps to reproduce, describe actual behavior, or add contextual details.

[JAMIE]
Fourth is dropdown.

[ALEX]
A dropdown gives a select menu of predefined options. It's great when you want consistent values, such as browser names, severity levels, proficiency levels, or screen reader choices.

[JAMIE]
And fifth is checkboxes.

[ALEX]
Checkboxes allow one or more confirmation items or option selections. They're useful for acknowledgments like "I searched existing issues" or "I can reproduce this in the latest version," and sometimes for multiple-choice-style selections where multiple values may apply.

[JAMIE]
How should learners choose the right field type?

[ALEX]
Ask what kind of answer you need. If you want instructions only, use markdown. If the response should be short and open-ended, use input. If it needs detail, use textarea. If the answer should come from a controlled list, use dropdown. If the user needs to confirm or select multiple items, use checkboxes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's build the accessibility bug report template conceptually.

[ALEX]
This is one of the most important parts of the chapter. A strong accessibility bug report template should gather the information maintainers actually need without overwhelming contributors.

[JAMIE]
What fields make that work?

[ALEX]
A good set might include Component Affected, so maintainers know where the problem lives. Your Assistive Technology Setup, so they know the screen reader, magnifier, browser, operating system, or other tools involved. Expected Behavior and Actual Behavior, so the gap is clear. Steps to Reproduce, so someone else can verify the issue. WCAG Success Criterion if known, which is optional but valuable for teams working against standards. Additional Context for anything else. And possibly a Before Submitting checklist.

[JAMIE]
What makes that template accessible, beyond just collecting accessibility-related information?

[ALEX]
Several things. Clear labels. Brief descriptions that explain why information is needed. Sensible required fields so users aren't blocked by nonessential details. Predictable field order. Controlled choices where helpful. And language that respects varying levels of expertise. For example, "WCAG Success Criterion if known" is much better than implying the reporter must be a standards expert.

[JAMIE]
That phrase "if known" is doing a lot of inclusive work.

[ALEX]
It is. It invites useful information without turning knowledge gaps into barriers.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also mentions a second template: a feature request form.

[ALEX]
Yes. That reinforces the idea that templates should fit the workflow. A feature request form might ask what problem the feature solves, who it helps, why current behavior is insufficient, possible approaches, and any accessibility considerations. The exact fields differ because the task differs.

[JAMIE]
And that leads into designing templates for your own projects.

[ALEX]
Right. Don't copy blindly. Look at issue patterns in your project. What information do maintainers repeatedly ask for? What information do contributors often forget? Which details help triage or reproduce? Your template should reflect those realities.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we leave templates, we also need to cover pull request templates.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Pull request templates guide contributors when proposing changes, not just when reporting issues. A PR template might include sections for Description, Type of Change, How to Test, Accessibility Considerations, and Related Issues.

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack those.

[ALEX]
Description explains what the PR does. Type of Change categorizes the work, such as bug fix, documentation update, new feature, or refactor. How to Test gives reviewers concrete steps to verify the change. Accessibility Considerations asks the author to think explicitly about keyboard support, screen reader impact, semantic structure, contrast, motion, or anything else relevant. Related Issues links the PR back to the issues it resolves or supports.

[JAMIE]
That accessibility section in a PR template is really important, because it nudges people to think about impact before merging.

[ALEX]
Yes. Good templates don't just collect text. They shape contributor behavior.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's move into the hands-on activities. First, using an existing template.

[ALEX]
In the first exercise, learners go to the Accessibility Agents repository's issues area. Then they open the New Issue flow and inspect the template chooser with a screen reader or other assistive technology.

[JAMIE]
What should they pay attention to there?

[ALEX]
Template names, descriptions, and whether the controls are understandable and easy to navigate. Then they select a template, move through the form fields, and notice how labels, descriptions, and required indicators are presented.

[JAMIE]
Then fill in the form.

[ALEX]
Yes, with realistic sample content. After that, preview the issue before submitting. That's a valuable step because it lets you catch missing details, formatting problems, or unclear wording. Then submit the issue and reflect: Did the template help? Were any fields confusing? Did the structure make the task easier?

[JAMIE]
That reflection step matters because we're not just consuming templates. We're learning to evaluate them.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The next exercise is adding the accessibility bug report template to your own fork. Walk us through that workflow.

[ALEX]
First, clone your fork to your machine. Second, open it in VS Code. Third, navigate to the templates folder, usually .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Fourth, create a new template file with a descriptive name.

[JAMIE]
Then paste in the YAML template.

[ALEX]
Right. Copy in the accessibility template YAML. Then verify the syntax carefully. YAML errors often come from indentation, misplaced dashes, or inconsistent spacing. After that, create a branch, commit your changes, and push.

[JAMIE]
And then test it on GitHub web.

[ALEX]
Yes. Open the repository on GitHub.com, activate New Issue, and make sure your template appears in the chooser. Launch it, inspect the fields, and confirm the rendered form matches your expectations.

[JAMIE]
Then comes a particularly important step for this audience: test with your screen reader.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Don't stop at "it loads." Check whether labels are understandable, whether descriptions are discoverable, whether required fields are clear, and whether the order makes sense in real navigation. If you can merge your branch afterward, that's optional depending on your workflow. The key checkpoint is that the template is present, valid, and usable.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then there's the upstream contribution exercise.

[ALEX]
Yes. Once your template is ready, create a pull request. Write a clear PR title and description. The source suggests organizing the PR body around questions like: What does this PR do? Why is this useful? How was this tested? And what related issue connects to it?

[JAMIE]
That mirrors the idea of a PR template, even if you're writing manually.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then review your PR before submitting, submit it, respond to feedback from maintainers, and celebrate your contribution.

[JAMIE]
That last part is not fluff.

[ALEX]
No, it's not. Shipping contribution infrastructure is real open source work.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's one more design exercise: creating a template for your own project from scratch.

[ALEX]
This is where the chapter shifts from imitation to authorship. First, choose a project. Second, identify recurring issue patterns. What kinds of reports show up repeatedly? Third, decide which fields are required. Ask yourself what maintainers truly need every time.

[JAMIE]
And then optional fields.

[ALEX]
Yes. Optional fields are for useful but nonessential information. Then write strong placeholders and help text. Good help text reduces confusion without overwhelming the contributor.

[JAMIE]
Then test locally.

[ALEX]
Right. Review the file, lint the YAML if needed, and inspect it carefully. Optionally deploy it to GitHub and ask a friend to try it, especially with assistive technology if possible. Finally, reflect on the design. Did your fields collect what matters? Did they avoid jargon? Did they reduce unnecessary effort?

[JAMIE]
So template design is really a user experience task.

[ALEX]
Very much so.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's circle back to the challenge evidence and completion process, because that's easy to skip over.

[ALEX]
Good point. After completing the challenge work, learners are supposed to open their assigned challenge issue and post a completion comment. The comment should indicate whether they analyzed the registration template, what context they remixed it for, whether the YAML validates, which repository contains the template, and whether they also created a Markdown version or tested in the chooser. Then they close the challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
That's useful evidence because it documents both the work and the quality checks.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What outcomes should learners expect by the end?

[ALEX]
They should understand template structure, including YAML frontmatter, field types, and validation. They should be able to analyze and remix professional templates. They should be able to create both YAML form and Markdown templates. They should understand why templates improve contribution quality. And they should appreciate how thoughtful templates reduce maintainer effort while helping contributors succeed.

[JAMIE]
And if someone gets stuck?

[ALEX]
A few likely sticking points are worth naming. If you can't find the registration template, double-check the repository path under .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. If your YAML fails, inspect indentation first. If the template doesn't appear in GitHub, confirm the filename and folder location, then push the branch and refresh the web view. If the form feels confusing with a screen reader, simplify labels and descriptions and retest.

[JAMIE]
And more broadly, compare your work to a known-good template rather than debugging in the abstract.

[ALEX]
Yes. Working from a professional example is one of the strongest learning patterns in this chapter.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Speaking of learning patterns, what's the deeper learning moment here?

[ALEX]
The learning moment is that contribution quality often depends less on contributor talent and more on workflow design. If you give people an accessible, well-structured form, you raise the floor for everyone. Templates are not bureaucracy. They are support.

[JAMIE]
And the learning pattern used here really is analyze, remix, create, test.

[ALEX]
Exactly. First read a real example closely. Then adapt it. Then create your own. Then test it in the actual environment. That sequence builds both confidence and judgment.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we end, let's talk about the Day 2 amplifier: the template builder agent.

[ALEX]
Yes. Later in the course, there's an agent called at-template-builder that helps generate templates in VS Code. Conceptually, it works by turning your description of a workflow into a draft issue or pull request template.

[JAMIE]
But this chapter makes sure you understand what good output should look like before using that tool.

[ALEX]
Right. Otherwise you'd get automation without judgment. In VS Code, the agent can help you draft, revise, and iterate faster. But it matters because it saves time only when you can review the result critically.

[JAMIE]
So the tool is an amplifier, not a substitute for understanding.

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Any final notes on sources or where learners should look when they want the official word?

[ALEX]
Yes. The authoritative references are GitHub's documentation about issue and pull request templates and GitHub's documentation on configuring issue templates for a repository. If behavior changes over time, those docs are the place to verify details. The chapter also points learners to related appendices like Markdown reference material and GitHub Actions context.

[JAMIE]
So the practical takeaway is: use the chapter to learn the workflow, and use the official docs to confirm implementation details.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And if you remember just one thing from today, let it be this: a good template is an accessibility tool, a communication tool, and a maintenance tool all at once.

[JAMIE]
Which is a pretty strong payoff for something that starts as "just a form."

[ALEX]
It really is. See you next time.

# Issue Templates
>
> **Listen to Episode 16:** [Issue Templates](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix Q: GitHub Actions](appendix-q-actions-workflows.md) | [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md) | [Appendix N: Advanced Search](appendix-n-advanced-search.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About issue and PR templates](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/using-templates-to-encourage-useful-issues-and-pull-requests/about-issue-and-pull-request-templates) | [GitHub Docs: Configuring issue templates](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/using-templates-to-encourage-useful-issues-and-pull-requests/configuring-issue-templates-for-your-repository)

## Structuring Contributions for Clarity and Quality

> Issue templates turn a blank text box into a guided form. They help contributors provide the information maintainers need, reduce back-and-forth, and make every issue immediately actionable. This guide teaches you what templates are, how to use the ones in [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents), and how to create your own - including an accessibility-specific bug report template.

## Prerequisites Checklist

### Challenge 14.1 Step-by-Step: Analyze the Registration Template

**Goal:** Understand how professional YAML form templates work by examining the one you filled out to register for this workshop.

**Where you are working:** GitHub.com - reading the template file in the [git-going-with-github](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github) repository.

**Estimated time:** 10-15 minutes.

**The Template:** [`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/workshop-registration.yml`](https://github.com/community-access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/workshop-registration.yml) - This is the form you filled out to register. It is a real, production template.

1. Open the template file on GitHub.com (use the link above).
2. Read the **YAML frontmatter** (top 5 lines) and identify:
   - `name` - what appears in the template chooser
   - `description` - helper text when users pick this template
   - `title` - auto-fills the issue title
   - `labels` - automatically adds labels to issues created with this template
3. Read the **field types** in the `body` section. Note the four types used:
   - `type: markdown` - display-only text (instructions)
   - `type: input` - single-line text field (name, email)
   - `type: dropdown` - list of options (proficiency level, screen reader choice)
   - `type: textarea` - multi-line text (questions/accommodations)
4. For each field, identify the **metadata**:
   - `id` - internal identifier (does not display to user)
   - `label` - what the user sees as the field name
   - `description` - helper text explaining what to fill in
   - `placeholder` - example text inside the field
   - `validations: required: true` - marks a field as required
5. Search the file for "accessible" - notice the description mentions that all fields work with screen readers. This is professional template thinking.
6. Compare: how is this different from a blank issue? A blank issue is a massive empty text box with no guidance. This template provides structured fields, helpful descriptions, and required/optional clarity.

**You are done when:** You can explain the purpose of each field type and why templates reduce back-and-forth questions.

## 1. What Is an Issue Template?

An issue template is a pre-filled Markdown file that appears when someone activates "New Issue." Instead of an empty editor, the contributor sees:

- Instructions explaining what information is needed
- Section headers guiding them through the report
- Checkboxes for conditions to verify
- Placeholder text showing the expected format

### Why they matter for accessibility projects

Accessibility bugs require specific context that general bug templates often omit:

- Which screen reader and version?
- Which browser and version?
- Which operating system?
- Which WCAG success criterion is affected?
- Does the issue affect all users or only those with specific assistive technology?

Without this context, maintainers ask follow-up questions - which delays the fix and uses everyone's time. A good accessibility template captures it all on the first submission.

## 2. How Templates Work on GitHub

Templates live in a specific folder in your repository:

### Description

Templates live inside your-repo/.github/. The ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ subfolder contains: bug_report.md (Markdown template), feature_request.md (Markdown template), accessibility-bug.yml (YAML form template), and config.yml (template chooser configuration). The pull_request_template.md file sits directly in .github/, not inside ISSUE_TEMPLATE/.

**Markdown templates (`.md`):** Traditional template format. Pre-fills a text editor with structured Markdown content. Contributors edit the template directly, replacing instructions and placeholder text with their own content.

**YAML form templates (`.yml`):** Modern form-based templates. Creates a proper form interface with labeled fields, dropdowns, checkboxes, and validation. Contributors fill in fields rather than editing freeform Markdown. Better for accessibility because each field has an explicit label announced by screen readers.

**`config.yml`:** Controls the template chooser page - what templates appear, what their descriptions say, whether an external link (like a discussion forum) appears as an option, and crucially, **whether contributors can bypass templates entirely with a blank issue**.

For accessibility projects, `config.yml` is important: disabling the blank issue option means every report arrives with the structure your project needs. A screen reader bug report without reproduction steps and AT version information is almost impossible to triage - the form prevents that by making those fields required.

### Example `config.yml`

```yaml
blank_issues_enabled: false
contact_links:
  - name: Community Discussion
    url: https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/discussions
    about: For questions and general discussion - not bugs
  - name: Security Vulnerability
    url: https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/security/advisories/new
    about: Please use private reporting for security issues
```

With `blank_issues_enabled: false`, the "Open a blank issue" link disappears from the template chooser. Contributors must use one of your structured templates or one of the contact links. This is one of the most effective ways to improve the quality of incoming issues in any project you maintain.

### Choosing Between Markdown and YAML Templates

> **See also:** [Appendix Q: GitHub Actions](appendix-q-actions-workflows.md) covers how templates connect to automated workflows.

Before creating a template, decide which format best suits your needs:

| Factor | Markdown Templates | YAML Form Templates |
| --------  | -------------------  | ---------------------  |
| **Best for** | Simple templates, freeform text | Structured data collection, accessibility |
| **Complexity** | Very simple to create | More complex, requires YAML knowledge |
| **Screen reader UX** | Announces as pre-filled text editor | Announces each field with explicit labels |
| **Validation** | None - contributors can delete anything | Can mark fields as required, validate input |
| **Flexibility** | Full Markdown formatting freedom | Limited to defined field types |
| **Data consistency** | Varies - contributors may skip sections | High - dropdowns ensure consistent values |
| **Learning curve** | Minimal | Moderate |
| **Maintenance** | Easy - just edit Markdown | More involved - must update YAML structure |

#### Use Markdown templates when

- You want contributors to have maximum flexibility in how they write
- The template is primarily instructional text with minimal structured data
- Your contributor base is comfortable with Markdown
- You don't need validation or required fields

#### Use YAML form templates when

- You need specific, structured information (OS, browser, version numbers)
- You want to guide less experienced contributors with dropdowns and validation
- Screen reader accessibility is critical (labeled form fields are more accessible)
- You want to ensure data consistency for automated triage or analysis
- You need required fields that contributors cannot skip

**For accessibility projects:** YAML form templates are strongly recommended. Accessibility bug reports require specific context (screen reader, browser, OS, version numbers) that Markdown templates rely on contributors to remember. Form templates make these fields explicit and required.

### Markdown Template Structure

A Markdown template consists of two parts:

**1. YAML Frontmatter** (between `---` delimiters)

Defines metadata about the template:

```yaml
name: Bug Report                    # Name shown in template chooser
about: Report a bug or error        # Description in template chooser
title: '[BUG] '                     # Pre-filled issue title (user can edit)
labels: ['bug', 'needs-triage']     # Auto-applied labels
assignees: ''                       # Auto-assigned maintainers (optional)
```

#### 2. Markdown Body

The template content that pre-fills the issue editor:

```markdown
## Describe the Bug
A clear and concise description of what the bug is.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Go to '...'
2. Click on '...'
3. Scroll down to '...'
4. See error

## Expected Behavior
What you expected to happen.

## Actual Behavior
What actually happened.

## Environment
- **OS:** [e.g. Windows 11, macOS Sonoma]
- **Browser:** [e.g. Chrome 124, Firefox 125]
- **Screen Reader:** [e.g. NVDA 2025.3.3, VoiceOver]

## Additional Context
Add any other context about the problem here.
```

### Markdown template tips

- Use `##` headings to create clear sections
- Use HTML comments `<!-- like this -->` for instructions that shouldn't appear in final issue
- Use `**Bold text**` for field names to make them stand out
- Use bullet lists or numbered lists for checklists
- Be specific: "Browser version (e.g. Chrome 124)" is better than "Browser"
- Include examples in brackets: `[e.g. ...]` helps contributors understand format

### When to use this Markdown version instead of YAML

- Your contributors are comfortable with Markdown and prefer editing text
- You want contributors to have more freedom in how they structure their report
- The template is for an internal project where you know all contributors
- You want a simpler template that's easier to modify later

### Markdown template accessibility considerations

- Checkboxes use `- [ ]` syntax (Markdown task lists)
- Instructions are in HTML comments `<!-- -->` so they don't clutter the final issue
- Bracket placeholders `[e.g. ...]` show expected format
- Section headings use `##` for clear document structure
- Screen readers can navigate by heading through the template

## 6. YAML Form-Based Templates

YAML templates create a proper form interface - labeled fields, dropdowns, checkboxes - rather than a pre-filled text editor. This is the preferred format for modern GitHub projects, especially those focused on accessibility.

### Why YAML Forms Are Better for Accessibility

**Explicit labels:** Each field has a `label:` that screen readers announce. In Markdown templates, users must infer structure from headings and placeholder text.

**Structured navigation:** Screen readers can navigate form fields with standard form navigation commands (`F` key in NVDA/JAWS, form controls in VoiceOver rotor).

**Required field validation:** Screen readers announce when a field is required before the user submits. Markdown templates have no validation.

**Consistent data:** Dropdowns provide options that screen readers can navigate (`Up/Down Arrow` to hear each choice). contributors don't have to guess valid values.

**Skip unreadable instructions:** HTML comments in Markdown templates (`<!-- -->`) can confuse some screen reader configurations. YAML `markdown` fields provide instruction text that renders as readable content, not editing noise.

### YAML Template Structure

A YAML form template consists of several parts:

```yaml
name: Issue Template Name         # Shows in template chooser
description: Longer description   # Shows in template chooser
title: "[TAG] "                   # Pre-filled issue title
labels: ["label1", "label2"]      # Auto-applied labels
assignees: ["username"]           # Auto-assigned (optional)
body:                             # Array of form fields
  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        Instructional text here

  - type: input
    id: unique-field-id
    attributes:
      label: Field Label
      description: Help text under the label
      placeholder: Placeholder text in the field
    validations:
      required: true
```

#### Top-level keys

- `name` (required): Template name in chooser
- `description` (required): Template description in chooser
- `title` (string): Pre-fills issue title, contributor can edit
- `labels` (array): Labels auto-applied when issue is created
- `assignees` (array): Usernames auto-assigned when issue is created
- `body` (array): The form fields (required)

```yaml
name: Accessibility Bug Report
description: Report an accessibility issue in Accessibility Agents' output or interface
title: "[A11Y] "
labels: ["accessibility", "needs-triage"]
body:
  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        Thank you for reporting an accessibility issue.
        Please fill in as much detail as possible.

  - type: dropdown
    id: screen-reader
    attributes:
      label: Screen Reader
      description: Which screen reader are you using?
      options:
        - NVDA (Windows)
        - JAWS (Windows)
        - VoiceOver (macOS)
        - VoiceOver (iOS)
        - TalkBack (Android)
        - Narrator (Windows)
        - Orca (Linux)
        - None
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: checkboxes
    id: checked-existing
    attributes:
      label: Before Submitting
      options:
        - label: I searched for existing issues and this is not a duplicate
          required: true
        - label: I am using the modern GitHub Issues experience (default since Jan 2026)
          required: false
```

### YAML Field Types Reference

GitHub supports several field types in YAML form templates. Each has specific attributes and uses:

#### 1. `markdown` - Instructional Text

Displays formatted Markdown content. Not editable by the contributor. Use for instructions, warnings, or explanations.

```yaml
- type: markdown
  attributes:
    value: |
      ## Before You Begin

      Please search for [existing issues](../issues) before submitting.
      Use this format for multi-line text.
```

##### Attributes

- `value` (required): Markdown content to display. Use `|` for multi-line text.

**No validation options** (static content)

**Screen reader note:** This content is announced as regular text. Screen reader users can read it with their reading commands before moving to the next field.

#### 2. `input` - Single-line Text Field

A single-line text input. Best for short answers like version numbers, URLs, or names.

```yaml
- type: input
  id: version
  attributes:
    label: Version Number
    description: Which version of the software are you using?
    placeholder: e.g., v2.4.1
  validations:
    required: true
```

##### Attributes

- `label` (required): Field label, announced by screen readers
- `description` (optional): Help text below the label
- `placeholder` (optional): Placeholder text inside the field

##### Validations

- `required` (boolean): Whether the field must be filled

**Screen reader announcement:** "Version Number, required, edit text, Which version of the software are you using?"

#### 3. `textarea` - Multi-line Text Area

A multi-line text input. Best for descriptions, reproduction steps, code snippets, or any long-form content.

```yaml
- type: textarea
  id: description
  attributes:
    label: Describe the Issue
    description: Provide as much detail as possible
    placeholder: |
      When I navigate to...
      The screen reader announces...
      I expected...
    value: |
      This text pre-fills the textarea.
      Contributors can edit or replace it.
    render: markdown
  validations:
    required: true
```

##### Attributes

- `label` (required): Field label
- `description` (optional): Help text
- `placeholder` (optional): Placeholder text (multi-line with `|`)
- `value` (optional): Pre-filled content (multi-line with `|`)
- `render` (optional): Syntax highlighting hint (e.g., `markdown`, `python`, `javascript`)

##### Validations

- `required` (boolean): Whether the field must be filled

**Accessibility tip:** Use `placeholder` for examples, `value` for pre-filled template text that contributors should edit.

#### 4. `dropdown` - Select Menu

A dropdown menu with predefined options. Contributors select one choice. Best for bounded answer spaces like OS, browser, or severity.

```yaml
- type: dropdown
  id: browser
  attributes:
    label: Browser
    description: Which browser are you using?
    options:
      - Google Chrome
      - Mozilla Firefox
      - Microsoft Edge
      - Apple Safari
      - Other
    multiple: false
  validations:
    required: true
```

##### Attributes

- `label` (required):Field label
- `description` (optional): Help text
- `options` (required): Array of choices (strings)
- `multiple` (boolean, default `false`): Whether user can select multiple options

##### Validations

- `required` (boolean): Whether a selection is required

##### Screen reader experience

1. Field is announced as "Browser, required, combo box"
2. Press `Down Arrow` or `Alt+Down` to expand the dropdown
3. `Up/Down Arrow` to navigate options
4. Screen reader announces each option
5. `Enter` or `Space` to select

**Accessibility note:** Dropdowns are more accessible than free text for bounded choices. Screen reader users can hear all options and select precisely.

#### 5. `checkboxes` - Checkbox Group

A group of checkboxes. Contributors can select multiple options or use as a verification checklist.

```yaml
- type: checkboxes
  id: prerequisites
  attributes:
    label: Before Submitting
    description: Please verify these items
    options:
      - label: I searched for existing issues
        required: true
      - label: I can reproduce this issue reliably
        required: true
      - label: I have attached relevant logs or screenshots
        required: false
```

##### Attributes

- `label` (required): Group label
- `description` (optional): Group description
- `options` (required): Array of checkbox objects

##### Each checkbox option

- `label` (required): Checkbox label (what the user sees)
- `required` (boolean, default `false`): Whether this checkbox must be checked

**No top-level validation** - validation is per-checkbox in `options`

##### Screen reader experience

1. Group label announced: "Before Submitting, Please verify these items"
2. Each checkbox announced as "I searched for existing issues, checkbox, not checked, required"
3. Screen reader users can check each box with `Space`

**Accessibility note:** Checkboxes with `required: true` prevent submission if unchecked. This enforces contribution guidelines (e.g., "search for duplicates first").

### YAML Field Types Summary Table

| Type | Best For | Key Attributes | Validations | Screen Reader Announced As |
| ------  | ----------  | ----------------  | -------------  | ----------------------------  |
| `markdown` | Instructions, warnings, explanations | `value` | None | Regular text content |
| `input` | Version numbers, URLs, short text | `label`, `placeholder` | `required` | "Edit text" or "Edit" |
| `textarea` | Descriptions, steps, code, long text | `label`, `placeholder`, `render` | `required` | "Multi-line edit" or "Text area" |
| `dropdown` | OS, browser, severity, bounded choices | `label`, `options`, `multiple` | `required` | "Combo box" or "Pop-up button" |
| `checkboxes` | Verification lists, multiple selections | `label`, `options` with per-item `required` | Per-checkbox | "Checkbox, not checked" |

#### Choosing the right field type

- If the answer is one of 2-10 known values → `dropdown`
- If the answer is a short string (1-2 words) → `input`
- If the answer is multiple sentences or a code block → `textarea`
- If the contributor must verify multiple conditions → `checkboxes` with `required: true`
- If you need to explain something → `markdown`

This template is itself an accessibility contribution:

- Every dropdown limits input to valid options, reducing errors for all users

- The WCAG dropdown educates as it collects data
- The "Additional Context" field is optional - a contributor with limited time can still file a useful report without this field

**Why this matters for your own projects:** Every open source project you create or maintain can have issue templates. A project with good templates gets better bug reports and feature requests - which means less back-and-forth and faster, more confident triage. The templates you create here are skills you carry to every repository you own.

### Designing Templates for Your Own Projects

When designing templates for a project you maintain, use these principles:

**Ask for the minimum that makes the report actionable.** Every optional field you add is a reason for a contributor with limited time to stop and not finish. Required fields should be information you genuinely cannot triage without.

**Use dropdowns over free text when the answer space is bounded.** "Which operating system?" should be a dropdown, not a text field. Bounded dropdowns reduce typos, inconsistent labeling, and fields left blank.

**Write textarea placeholders as examples, not instructions.** A placeholder that says "e.g., When I navigate to the Issues tab using NVDA in Chrome on Windows 11..." teaches the contributor what a good answer looks like. A placeholder that says "Describe the issue here" does not.

**Include a pre-submission checklist.** Even one checkbox - "I searched for existing issues" - reduces duplicate reports significantly. The checklist also reinforces community norms: the act of checking a box is more memorable than reading a line of text.

**Test every template with your screen reader before committing.** Navigate through the form, tab through all fields, confirm every label is announced correctly, and verify that required-field errors are surfaced in a way a screen reader user will encounter before submitting.

### Exercise D - Design a Template for Your Own Project

**Your Mission:** Apply everything you've learned to design a template for a repository you own, maintain, or plan to create.

**What You'll Learn:** How to make design decisions about required vs. optional fields, field types, and how to test your template with real users.

**Time estimate:** 30-45 minutes (can be done after the workshop)

#### Part 1: Choose Your Project

##### What to do

1. Think of a repository you have a personal connection to:
   - A project you own or maintain
   - A project you contribute to regularly
   - A project you plan to create (even if just in your head)
   - A project that's important to your workplace
2. **Write down the project name** and briefly why chose it:

   ```text
   Project: [name]
   Why it matters to me: [1 sentence]

   Current state: Exists, I maintain it
                  Exists, I contribute to it
                  I'm planning to create it
                  Other: [describe]
   ```

##### What success looks like

- You have a specific project in mind (not generic)
- You can articulate why you care about it

#### Part 2: Identify Issue Patterns

**Your task:** Study the issues your project receives (or would receive) to understand what information is most valuable.

##### What to do

##### If your project already has issues

1. Open your issue list in GitHub
2. **Read the last 5-10 issues** (or all open issues if fewer)
3. For each issue, ask yourself:
   - What problem was the reporter describing?
   - What information helped you (or would help) understand the issue?
   - What information was *missing* that you had to ask for?
4. **Write down 3-5 patterns:**

   ```text
   Issue Type 1: [what kind of issues are most common?]
   - Essential info needed: [what always helps?]
   - Often missing: [what do you always have to ask for?]

   Issue Type 2: [second most common type]
   - Essential info needed: [what?]
   - Often missing: [what?]
   ```

##### If your project doesn't exist yet or has no issues

1. Think about the *type* of issues you'd want to receive:
   - Bug reports?
   - Feature requests?
   - Documentation improvements?
   - All of the above?
2. For each type, ask: "If someone reported this issue, what would I need to know?"
3. Write down:

   ```text
   Issue Type 1: [e.g., "Bug Report"]
   - Essential info needed: [e.g., "What OS? Browser? Steps to reproduce?"]
   - Questions I'd ask: [What follow-ups would I need?]

   Issue Type 2: [e.g., "Feature Request"]
   - Essential info needed: [e.g., "What problem does this solve?"]
   - Questions I'd ask: [e.g., "Who else has asked for this?"]
   ```

##### What success looks like

- You've identified at least 2-3 issue types
- For each type, you know what information is crucial vs. nice-to-have

#### Part 3: Design Your Required Fields

**Your task:** List the fields you absolutely need to understand an issue.

##### What to do

**Rule:** Keep required fields minimal. If a field is required, you genuinely cannot triage without it.

1. Create a table:

   ```
   Field Name -- Type (dropdown/input/textarea) -- Why Required? -- Options (if dropdown)
   [name]     -- [type]                        -- [reason]      -- [choices]
   ```

2. For each issue type from Part 2, add 2-4 required fields:

   **Example for "Bug Report":**

   | Field | Type | Why? | Options |
   | -------  | ------  | ------  | ---------  |
   | Component | dropdown | "I have 5 components; knowing which is affected saves triage time" | Component A, B, C, D, E |
   | Steps to Reproduce | textarea | "I cannot fix what I cannot replicate" | (free text) |
   | OS | dropdown | "Bugs are often OS-specific" | Windows, macOS, Linux |

3. **Write down at least 2 required fields:**

   ```text
   Required Field 1: [name]
   - Type: [dropdown / input / textarea?]
   - Why is it required? [explain as if to the issue reporter]
   - If dropdown, options: [list them]

   Required Field 2: [name]
   - Type: [type]
   - Why is it required? [explain]
   - If dropdown, options: [list them]
   ```

##### What success looks like

- You have 2-4 required fields
- Each has a clear reason (not arbitrary)
- You can explain to someone why each field is required

#### Part 4: Design Your Optional Fields

**Your task:** Add optional fields that would be helpful but aren't blocking.

##### What to do

1. **Brainstorm nice-to-have information:**
   - Information that's helpful but you could triage without it
   - Information that helps you prioritize or assign the issue
   - Information that provides missing context

2. **Example optional fields for a bug report:**
   - Environment details (CPU, RAM, versions of dependencies)
   - Screenshots or links
   - Workarounds the reporter has found
   - When the issue started happening

3. **Write down at least 2 optional fields:**

   ```text
   Optional Field 1: [name]
   - Type: [dropdown / input / textarea / checkboxes?]
   - Why include it? [what does it help with?]

   Optional Field 2: [name]
   - Type: [type]
   - Why include it? [what insight does it provide?]
   ```

4. **For each field, decide:**
   - Should this be a dropdown (bounded choices) or free text (open-ended)?
   - If dropdown, list the options
   - If textarea, what's a helpful placeholder or example?

##### What success looks like

- You have 2-3 optional fields in addition to required ones
- Each optional field would genuinely help, but you could still triage without it
- Your template is neither overwhelming nor too sparse (aim for 5-7 fields total)

#### Part 5: Write Field Placeholders and Help Text

**Your task:** For each field, write helpful placeholder or description text that guides the reporter.

##### What to do

For each required and optional field, draft:

1. **Field label** (the visible name)
2. **Description** (short help text)
3. **Placeholder** (example of what to type, for input/textarea fields)

##### Examples

```text
Field: "Steps to Reproduce"
Description: "Numbered list of actions that trigger the bug"
Placeholder: "1. Open the settings menu
2. Click 'Advanced Options'
3. Toggle the switch
4. The app crashes"

Field: "Expected Behavior"
Description: "What should happen if everything worked correctly?"
Placeholder: "The settings should save silently and the app should remain open"
```

##### Write these for at least 3 of your fields

```text
Field 1: [name]
Description: [guidance for the reporter]
Placeholder: [example of good input]

Field 2: [name]
Description: [guidance]
Placeholder: [example]

Field 3: [name]
Description: [guidance]
Placeholder: [example]
```

##### What success looks like

- Placeholder text shows a real example, not just "e.g., enter text here"
- Description explains *why* you're asking, not just *what*
- An inexperienced reporter could read these and understand what you need

#### Part 6: Test Your Template Locally

**Your task:** Create a draft YAML template file and test it with your screen reader.

##### What to do

1. **Create a text file** with your template in YAML format. Use Section 6 as a template:
   - Start with the frontmatter (`name:`, `description:`, `title:`, `labels:`)
   - Add your fields in the `body:` section
   - Use appropriate field types (input, textarea, dropdown, checkboxes)

2. **Save it locally** (not yet in GitHub):
   - Name it: `[your-project-name]-template.yml`
   - Save it to your desktop or a projects folder

3. **Open it in VS Code** and check:
   - Is the YAML syntax correct? (no red squiggles)
   - Does every field have an `id`, `label`, and `attributes`?
   - Are required fields in a `validations:` block?

4. **Test the structure:**
   - Print it out or read it aloud
   - Does your field order make sense? (Related fields together?)
   - Are required fields grouped before optional?
   - Is any field confusing or unclear?

5. **With your screen reader:**
   - Open the YAML file in your editor
   - Navigate through it with your reader
   - Can you understand the structure: name, description, then body with fields?
   - Are the field labels clear?

##### If you find issues

- Reorder fields for clarity
- Simplify confusing help text
- Remove fields that seem redundant
- Save your changes

##### What success looks like

- Your YAML file has no syntax errors
- You can read through it and understand the template flow
- A screen reader user could navigate through the structure

#### Part 7: (Optional) Deploy to GitHub and Test with a Friend

**Your task:** Upload your template to a GitHub repository and test it with a colleague or friend.

##### What to do

This is optional but powerful - real user testing is the best validation.

1. **Upload your template** to a test repository:
   - Create a test branch in a personal repo
   - Add your template file to `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`
   - Push the branch

2. **Ask a colleague or friend:**
   - "Could you try filing an issue using this template?"
   - "What did you find confusing?"
   - "Did any required fields feel unnecessary?"
   - "Were the descriptions helpful?"

3. **Collect feedback:**
   - What worked well?
   - What was confusing?
   - Did they skip any optional fields? (If yes, consider removing them)
   - Would they suggest different field options?

4. **Refine your template** based on their feedback

#### Part 8: Reflect on Your Template Design

**Your task:** Document what you learned from this exercise.

##### What to do

Write answers to these questions:

1. **Decision-making:** Which field did you debate including? Why did you finally decide yes or no?

   ```text
   Field: [name]
   Debate: [why was this hard to decide?]
   Decision: [required / optional / removed]
   Reason: [what made you decide?]
   ```

2. **Trade-offs:** You can't ask for everything without overwhelming reporters. What information did you choose *not* to ask for? Why?

   ```text
   Information I didn't include: [example]
   Why I chose not to ask: [explanation]
   Would I change this? [yes/no] + why
   ```

3. **Iteration:** If you had user feedback (from Part 7), what did you learn?

   ```text
   Feedback: [what did your friend/colleague say?]
   Change you made: [how did you refine?]
   Why it helped: [what improved?]
   ```

4. **Real-world readiness:** Would you actually deploy this template to a real project?

   ```text
   Readiness: Yes, I'm confident
              Maybe, with more testing
              No, I need to rethink some fields
   Next step: [what would you do next?]
   ```

##### What success looks like

- You can articulate why you made each design decision
- You understand the trade-offs between comprehensive and overwhelming
- You recognize where you'd improve with more user feedback

This skill - understanding what information *actually* matters - is what makes great templates. The YAML syntax is just the delivery mechanism. The hard part is the thinking you did in Parts 1-5.

### You've Completed the Template Exercises

You now:

1. Understand templates from the user perspective (Exercise A)
2. Can create and deploy templates yourself (Exercise B)
3. Know how to contribute upstream (Exercise C)
4. Can design templates with real thinking behind them (Exercise D)

In **Chapter 16 (Accessibility Agents)**, you'll see how the `@template-builder` agent automates the YAML writing part - but *you* bring the design thinking from this exercise. The agent generates YAML; you decide what questions to ask.

## 10. Day 2 Amplifier: The Template Builder Agent

Everything you just learned - field types, YAML structure, accessibility testing - is core GitHub knowledge. Now see how Accessibility Agents amplifies it.

Our 6th agent, **@template-builder**, is an interactive wizard that generates issue templates guided by your answers to simple questions. Instead of writing YAML by hand, you answer prompts and the agent produces a production-ready template in seconds.

### How It Works

#### In VS Code

```text
You: @template-builder create accessibility template
Agent: [Ask Questions interface]
  • Template name? → "Accessibility Bug Report"
  • What's this for? → "Report screen reader and keyboard issues"
  • First field? → "Screen Reader (dropdown)"
  • Options? → "NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack, Other"
  • Required? → "Yes"
  [... continues field by field]
Agent: Here's your YAML template [syntax-highlighted code block]
```

Then you copy, paste to `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/your-template.yml`, commit, and done.

### Why It Matters

| Approach | Time | Expertise | Error Rate |
| ----------  | ------  | -----------  | -----------  |
| Manual YAML | 15-20 min | High (YAML syntax) | Medium (typos, missing colons) |
| Copy-Paste Example | 10-15 min | Medium | Low (if example is good) |
| Agent-Guided | 2-3 min | Low (just describe) | Very Low (structured output) |

The Template Builder does not teach you to design templates - Section 5 taught you that. It automates the mechanical part: translating your decisions into working YAML.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.
